Very quickly on the trade-offs (high level):
- Hosted API (pay-as-you-go): fastest to start, predictable dev experience, good for low-volume / variable workloads. Unit price is higher but no infra ops. Good for validating functional requirements.
- Dedicated (reserved capacity): lower effective $/1M at commit, better tail latency and throughput for sustained peak loads. Requires a commitment window but gives predictable unit economics.
- Private (VPC / on-prem): used for regulated workloads; pricing and ops are bespoke.

On batching vs streaming:
- Larger batches increase throughput and reduce $/token materially, but add tail latency. If P95 latency is a hard SLO for some endpoints, we recommend smaller batch sizes or a small dedicated pool for those endpoints.
- Streaming helps perceived latency for long responses (users see tokens earlier) but increases network/CPU overhead and can raise unit cost slightly.

Jessica —

Great, thanks for the clarifications — appreciate the budget transparency. Below are the concrete numbers and recommendations tailored to the volumes you mentioned. These are ballpark estimates to help procurement and infra decide:

1) Ballpark unit economics (per 1M tokens) — illustrative ranges
- Hosted API, balanced model (default): $18–$24 per 1M tokens
- Hosted API, low-latency tier (pinning on faster kernels / smaller batch windows / reserved runtime): $28–$40 per 1M tokens
- Dedicated (12-mo commit, 50% utilization assumed): $9–$15 per 1M tokens (depends on commit size and model family)
- Private / on-prem: typically quoted case-by-case — unit economics comparable to dedicated at scale but with additional infra fees.

Notes on these numbers:
- Hosted low-latency tier increases unit cost because we bias toward smaller batch windows, more pre-warmed capacity, and lower tail latency guarantees.
- Dedicated reduces $/token mainly through reserved GPU utilization and larger batching across customer traffic. Hitting the lower bound (~$9/1M) typically requires a >12-month, mid-to-high commit (we commonly see 50–150M tokens/month equivalents across the pool across customers). For your expected ~30M/mo, we’d likely see mid-range dedicated economics (~$11–$13/1M) with a 12-mo commit.

2) Streaming vs non-streaming impact
- Streaming (token-by-token responses) improves perceived latency for long responses but increases RPC round-trips & memory pressure. Expect a ~10–20% increase in effective unit cost relative to non-streamed responses for the same model and tokens, mostly due to less headroom for batching and slightly higher CPU overhead.

3) Batching guidance
- For your real-time agent assist path: recommend small batch windows (e.g., max batch size 8–16, max wait 10–20ms) on a low-latency tier or a small dedicated pool. This hits your P50/P95 targets with minimal cost inflation.
- For async enrichment: use larger batch windows and dedicated capacity to lower cost (can reduce $/token by 30–50% relative to low-latency hosted).

Recommended pilot configuration
- 3-week pilot: Hosted low-latency tier for agent-assist (config above) + a small dedicated pool for async enrichment.
- Expected pilot volume: 12–15M tokens total across both paths.
- Estimated monthly run-rate if scaled to 30M (mix 60% real-time, 40% async): ~$11k–$16k/month depending on whether you choose to move agent-assist to dedicated.

Proposed commercial option for pilot
- 30% off hosted list rates for the first month of pilot to accelerate evaluation.
- If you commit to a 12-mo dedicated contract after pilot, we’ll apply usage credits that further reduce the first 3 months.

I’ve attached a simple pricing-model.xlsx with scenario tables and included a draft pilot SOW. Docs: pricing-model.xlsx, pilot-sow-draft.pdf.
